title: Contactless terahertz mapping of wafer-scale superconducting NbTiN thin films
authors: Yayi Lin, Marc Neis, Marcello Pio Guardascione, Janine Lorenz, Thomas J. Smart, F. Stefan Tautz, Felix Lüpke, Frederik Bolle, Martin Dressel, Rami Barends, Pavel A. Bushev, Marc Scheffler
abstract: For large-scale superconducting quantum technology, e.g. quantum computing, the homogeneity of wafer-scale superconducting thin films is vital for consistent performance of the fabricated devices. Terahertz (THz) spectroscopy as a contactless and non-destructive measurement technique is a powerful tool to characterize the superconducting films. In this work, a set of niobium titanium nitride (NbTiN) thin films on 4-inch and 6-inch silicon wafers, grown via plasma-enhanced magnetron sputtering, are investigated via THz spectroscopy: full wafers are mapped at room temperatures and exemplary segments are characterized at cryogenic temperatures. The deviations in observed sheet resistance depend on the used deposition device and the film thickness. While the deviations in superconducting sheet kinetic inductance match those of the normal-state sheet resistance, the critical temperature and energy gap exhibit little variation. This THz mapping technique demonstrates the feasibility of evaluating wafer-scale superconducting thin films before lithography, facilitating preparation of the thin films for reproducible device fabrication.
summary: This paper demonstrates a powerful, contactless technique using Terahertz spectroscopy to map the homogeneity of superconducting $	ext{NbTiN}$ thin films across entire wafers. By correlating spatial variations in normal-state resistance ($R_s$) with changes in the superconducting kinetic inductance ($L_k$), the authors provide a crucial pre-fabrication quality control method for quantum computing components.
main_problem: The primary goal is to ensure the homogeneity of superconducting thin films across entire wafers for reliable use in large-scale quantum devices.
main_result: THz mapping proves that local variations in normal-state resistance ($R_s$) correlate with deviations in the zero-temperature kinetic inductance ($L_{k0}$), enabling pre-lithography quality control.
method: The study employs contactless Terahertz (THz) spectroscopy, combining room-temperature frequency-domain mapping for $R_s$ and cryogenic time-domain measurements to probe superconducting gaps and kinetic inductance.
model_or_system: The system involves Niobium Titanium Nitride ($	ext{NbTiN}$) thin films on silicon wafers. Analysis relies on the Drude model for normal state resistance and Mattis-Bardeen theory for extracting the superconducting energy gap ($2\Delta$).
key_observables: Sheet resistance ($R_s$), critical temperature ($T_c$), superconducting energy gap ($2\Delta$), and sheet kinetic inductance ($L_k$).
important_parameters: Wafer sizes (4-inch, 6-inch), THz frequency range ($\sim 0.1 - 3 	ext{ THz}$), and temperature regimes (room to cryogenic).
main_assumptions: The extraction of $R_s$ from raw spectra assumes the scattering rate is much larger than in the THz regime; fitting superconducting properties uses established BCS/Mattis-Bardeen models.
figures_summary: Figures show room-temperature maps of sheet resistance deviations ($\delta R_s$) and cryogenic measurements comparing spatial distributions of $2\Delta$ and $L_{k0}$ across different wafer locations.
paper_structure: The work progresses from establishing the need for homogeneity in quantum technology, detailing the THz mapping methodology (room vs. cryo), presenting results showing correlations between normal-state and superconducting property variations, and concluding on the technique's feasibility as a pre-screening tool.
why_interesting: While focused on materials characterization rather than fundamental AMO physics, the use of non-contact THz spectroscopy to probe collective quantum phenomena (superconducting condensate) at wafer scale is highly relevant for developing superconducting quantum hardware.
